heading: The brake that the tumor borrows
exactSourceText: Tumors often display PD-L1 *because* T cells are attacking them. T cells that recognize a tumor release interferon gamma, and interferon gamma induces PD-L1 on nearby tumor and immune cells. This is called **[adaptive immune resistance](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/tumor-immunology/adaptive-immune-resistance)**: the brake is pulled in response to the attack ([Taube et al., 2012](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22461641/)). That is why PD-L1 staining and a [lymphocyte-rich "hot" pattern](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/tumor-immunology/hot-excluded-cold-tumor) often travel together.

heading: The cost: immune-related adverse events
exactSourceText: Releasing a brake that protects healthy tissue can cause inflammation in any organ. These [immune-related adverse events (irAEs)](/wiki/education/concepts/therapeutics/toxicities-and-supportive-care/immune-related-adverse-event) usually appear during treatment but can start after it ends. Across 2,799 patients given pembrolizumab alone in trials, hypothyroidism occurred in 8% and adrenal insufficiency in 0.8%. In KEYNOTE-522, pembrolizumab was stopped for adverse reactions in 20% of patients, and the label asks for blood cortisol checks before surgery in this setting ([FDA label, sections 5.1 and 6.1](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2026/125514s194lbl.pdf)).
